entry.title: About Git
entry.content:
This will be a full course and reminder about Git. It was inspired from theprimeagen course on bootdev

Table of Contents

  • Setup
  • Start
  • Branching
  • Merge
  • Rebase
  • Undoing changes
  • Remote
  • Fork
  • Conflicting changes
  • Rebase conflicts
  • Squashing
  • Stash
  • Revert
  • Cherry pick
  • Bisect
  • Worktree
  • Tags
  • Extra commands

Setup

Porcelain (the most used commands) and plumbing (rare to need them) commands.

To see the configs you are using:

git config --list

Usually you configure everything with --global, so you don’t have to do it every time, unless you want a different setting locally.

git config --global init.defaultBranch master

(--add if you already have something else)

Start

mkdir foldername
cd foldername

git init # repo initialised

A file can be:

  • untracked
  • staged
  • committed

You can check by:

git status

Staging

git add filename
# or
git add . # add everything within that directory only (nothing above it)

Commit

A commit is a snapshot of the repository at a given point in time.

git commit -m "msg"

Log

git log

It shows:

  • Who made a commit
  • When the commit was made
  • What was changed

For better visualisation:

git --no-pager log -n 10 --oneline --parents --graph

Hashes

What affects a hash:

  • The commit message
  • The author’s name and email
  • The date and time
  • Parent commit hashes

Git uses SHA-1 (newer versions of Git support SHA-256 as an optional alternative, but SHA-1 is still the default almost everywhere).

Plumbing

All the data in a Git repository is stored directly in the hidden .git directory. That includes all the commits, branches, tags, and other objects.

Git saves everything as raw compressed bytes (that’s why it’s small). You’d need a tool like xxd to view it directly.

You can also use git cat-file -p hash to get roughly the same information in a readable form.

Trees and blobs

Tree: Git’s way of storing a directory Blob: Git’s way of storing a file

Storing data

Git stores an entire snapshot of files at every commit (not just the changes).

             Git Objects
                  │
      ┌───────────┼────────────┐
      │           │            │
    Blob        Tree        Commit
                                 │
                              (Tag)
  • Blob: file contents
  • Tree: directory structure
  • Commit: snapshot metadata
  • Tag: named reference

Config

git config --add --global user.name "Ahpatsum"
git config --add --global user.email "ahpatsum@mus.com"

These are stored in ~/.gitconfig, or you can store them locally using --local, in which case they go in .git/config instead.

To view the local config:

git config --list --local
# or
cat .git/config

It’s stored as:

[section]
    key = value

To view a certain value:

git config --get <key>

where <key> is <section>.<keyname>.

Unset

To remove a key:

git config --unset section.key
Duplicates

Git config allows duplicate keys under the same section (similar to a list rather than a single value). To purge all instances of a key from your configuration:

git config --unset-all section.key
Remove a section
git config --remove-section section

Location

Usually you will only need:

  • global: ~/.gitconfig
  • local: .git/config

There’s also:

  • system: /etc/gitconfig
  • worktree: .git/config.worktree — a file that configures Git for part of a project.

The hierarchy: System → Global → Local → Worktree

Branching

A Git branch allows you to keep track of different changes separately. The last commit on a branch is called the branch tip.

To check which branch you are on:

git branch

On GitHub, it’s usually main used as the default branch instead of master.

To set a specific default branch name for this repository, you can use:

git branch -m master main
# or
git config --add --local init.defaultBranch main

New branch

To create and switch to a new branch:

git branch my_new_branch
# or
git switch -c my_new_branch # create it and switch to it

The old command is git checkout -b.

To just switch: git switch branch

To visualize more you can use --decorate=full, but --oneline --graph does the same job for most cases.

Merge

Once you are happy with the changes in your feature, you want to merge them back into the main branch.

Merge commits

Merge base: the most common ancestor.

How it works:

  • Find the merge base commit
  • Replay the changes from new_branch onto main, starting from the best common ancestor
  • Record the result as a new commit
  • The new commit has 2 parents in this case
git merge new_branch # you should be on main

After merging, visualize it nicely with git log --oneline --decorate --graph --parents.

Fast-forward merge

The simplest way to merge:

      C  new_feature
     /
A - B   main

The merge base is also the branch tip of main.

git merge new_feature — no merge commit is created.

git branch -d old_feature — to delete a feature branch once it’s merged.

Rebase

Rebase changes the merge base to the branch tip, without merging them, and leaves the possibility of a fast-forward merge later on.

You can create a new_feature branch with HEAD pointing to a specific commit:

git switch -c feature COMMITHASH

The command:

git rebase main

Merge vs. rebase: An advantage of merge is that it preserves the true history of the project. It shows when branches were merged and where. One disadvantage is that it can create a lot of merge commits, which can make history harder to read.

A linear history is generally easier to read, understand, and work with.

Warning: You should never rebase a public/shared branch onto anything else. Other developers have it checked out, and if you rewrite its history, you’ll cause problems for them.

However, on your own branch, you can rebase onto other branches as much as you want.

Undoing changes

git reset –soft

git reset --soft COMMITHASH

Undoes the last commit(s) but keeps the changes in the index (staged) and working tree.

--soft is useful if you want to go back to a previous commit but keep all your changes. Committed changes become uncommitted and staged, while already-uncommitted changes stay as they were.

If it’s in recent history: git reset --soft HEAD~1

git reset –hard

Undoes everything:

git reset --hard COMMITHASH

Danger: git reset --hard undoes the commit and deletes the corresponding file changes for good.

Remote

In Git, another repo is called a “remote”. The convention is to name it origin when it’s the “authoritative source of truth” (e.g. on GitHub).

git remote add <name> <uri> # uri can be a local path too

Fetch

git fetch # bring everything from the remote into the current repo

To see the remote’s history: git log origin/main

Merge

Just as we merge branches within a single local repo, we can also merge branches between local and remote repos.

git merge remote/branch

You need to fetch + merge to bring all the remote repo’s content into your local copy.

GitHub

Git ≠ GitHub. Add a remote:

git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo.git

To make sure it works: git ls-remote

Push

git push origin main # push local main's commits to origin's main

Alt options: git push origin <localbranch>:<remotebranch>

Pull

Fetching is nice, but most of the time we want the actual file changes from a remote repo, not just the metadata:

git pull [<remote>/<branch>]

Set git config --add --local pull.rebase false to avoid ambiguity/problems when merging on pull.

Pull request

When you add a new_feature, commit changes, and push, you can open a pull request on GitHub to propose merging your branch into main.

Workflow

Keep stuff on GitHub

Keep all serious projects on GitHub. That way you always have a backup, and if you’re on another computer, you can just clone the repo and get back to work.

Rebase vs. merge

You can configure Git to rebase by default on pull, rather than merge, to keep a linear history:

git config --global pull.rebase true
Solo workflow
  • Make changes to files
  • git add .
  • git commit -m "msg"
  • git push origin main

git log, git reset, and a few others are useful from time to time, but this is the core loop.

Team workflow
  • Update your local main branch: git pull origin main
  • Check out a new branch for your changes: git switch -c new_feature
  • Make changes to files
  • git add .
  • git commit -m "comment"
  • git push origin <branchname> (push to the new branch, not main)
  • Open a pull request on GitHub to merge your changes into main
  • Once approved, click “Merge” on GitHub
  • Delete your feature branch, and repeat for the next set of changes

.gitignore

Files you don’t want to commit, like .env files or build artifacts.

If you want to ignore something locally without adding it to the shared .gitignore, edit .git/info/exclude instead.

Nested .gitignore

Your .gitignore file doesn’t need to live only at the root of your project. It’s common to have multiple .gitignore files in different directories — a nested one only applies to the directory it’s in and its subdirectories.

Patterns

It would be rough if .gitignore only accepted exact file paths. Luckily, it supports:

  • Wildcards: *.txt
  • Rooted patterns: /main.py — patterns starting with / are anchored to the directory containing the .gitignore file, not its subdirectories
  • Negation: *.txt then !important.txt

Tips

  • To change your last commit message: git commit --amend (rewrites the hash — this is destructive/history-altering, avoid on shared branches).
  • git reset --soft is handy any time you want to uncommit without losing changes (e.g., to re-commit differently instead of rebasing).

Fork

A fork is a copy of a repository. Forking lets you freely experiment with changes without affecting the original project.

Forking is not a Git operation — it’s a feature offered by hosting services like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket. It’s essentially a copy that stays linked to the original via metadata.

Clone

git clone uri
cd repo
# make changes

PRs from a fork

  1. Fork their repo into your account
  2. Clone your fork locally
  3. Create a new branch
  4. Make changes
  5. Commit and push to your fork’s remote branch
  6. Open a pull request from your_username/repo:your_feature into original_owner/repo:main

The original owner can then review and merge your changes straight from your fork.

  • Fork if you want to contribute.
  • Clone if you just want to experiment.

It’s worth adding an upstream remote to keep up with the latest version of a repo you’ve forked:

git remote add upstream https://github.com/ORIGINAL_OWNER/ORIGINAL_REPO.git

This helps you avoid conflicts before opening a PR.

Reflog

“Reference log.” Reflog uses a different format to show the history of a branch or HEAD. The difference from log is that if you do a reset, it won’t show in log, but it will show in reflog.

Recovery

To recover something lost:

  • Use git reflog to find the commit hash
  • Use git cat-file -p COMMITHASH to find the tree, then find the blob hash for the file and print it out (same command, walking tree → blob)

A cleaner way to recover a whole branch state:

git merge <commitish>

<commitish> is anything that resolves to a commit (branch, tag, commit hash, HEAD@{1}, etc.)

git --no-pager reflog # find the entry you want
git merge HEAD@{1}    # or whatever index is shown

Conflicting changes

A merge conflict happens when two commits change the same line and Git can’t automatically decide which change to keep. This typically happens when the two commits aren’t in a parent-child relationship.

If you have a conflict and want to bail out: git merge --abort

Edit the file

Resolving conflicts is a manual process. Git marks the conflicted sections in the file:

<<<<<<< HEAD   (your current branch)
=======        (separator)
>>>>>>> main   (the incoming branch)

Resolution

After manually editing the conflicting file(s), add and commit the changes. This tells Git you’ve resolved the conflict and it can continue with the merge.

⚠️ Make sure to remove all conflict markers before committing.

Back to main

To go back to before the merge: git reset --hard HEAD~1

  • To help avoid future merge conflicts: git config --global rerere.enabled true
  • Once resolved, switch to main (ours) and fast-forward merge in the other branch (theirs), then delete the merged branch.

Multi-conflict

If you want to make a change and commit it without changing the commit message: git commit --amend --no-edit

Checkout conflict

git diff — to see the differences between commits.

You can use git checkout to choose which version of a file to keep:

git checkout --ours filepath
git checkout --theirs filepath
git add .
git commit -m "msg"

No merge commits

When resolving merge conflicts, Git doesn’t auto-generate the standard Merge branch 'main' into new_feature message — you have to write one manually. That makes sense: Git doesn’t know what you did to resolve the conflict, so it nudges you to document it yourself.

Rebase conflicts

Full disclosure: a lot of rebase’s bad reputation comes from conflicts. It’s nothing you can’t handle with a bit of practice.

Rebasing feels scarier because it rewrites Git history — if you’re not careful, you can lose work (though usually recoverable via reflog). But once you understand what’s going on, it keeps your history (and your team’s) cleaner and easier to follow.

--ours always refers to the branch you’re rebasing onto (e.g. main). git branch will show (no branch, rebasing ...) while a rebase is in progress.

“Accept incoming changes” = git checkout --theirs “Accept current change” = git checkout --ours

Example — preserving main’s version of a file:

git checkout --ours filepath
git rebase --continue # continue the rebase
git log --oneline --graph --parents

If there was a commit you made but chose to discard in favor of main’s version, that commit is simply dropped from history.

Repeat resolution setup

A common complaint about rebase is having to manually resolve the same conflict repeatedly — especially with long-running feature branches, or multiple branches being rebased onto main.

→ rerere to the rescue.

git rerere stands for “reuse recorded resolution.” It lets Git remember how you resolved a conflict hunk, so the next time it sees the same conflict, Git can resolve it automatically.

To enable it: git config --local rerere.enabled true

To force-delete a branch: git branch -D useless_feature

Accidental commit

If you accidentally commit the resolution of a rebase conflict (instead of running --continue):

git reset --soft HEAD~1 # undo the commit

Then simply continue the rebase as normal with git rebase --continue.

Squashing

Every dev team has different standards and opinions on how to use Git: a single commit per feature, or a series of small, focused commits.

To do the first, you’ll need to “squash” your commits together — useful for a clean history, and it also makes it easier to revert a change when the problem is spread across several commits/merges. Squashing is done with git rebase.

  1. Start an interactive rebase: git rebase -i HEAD~n, where n is the number of commits to squash.
  2. Git opens your editor with a list of commits. Change pick to squash (or s) for all but the first commit.
  3. Save and close the editor.

The -i flag stands for interactive — it lets you edit commit history before Git applies the changes. HEAD~n references the last n commits.

Why does rebase squash? Rebase is all about replaying changes. When you rebase onto a specific commit (HEAD~n), you’re telling Git to replay all the changes from the current branch on top of that commit — and the interactive flag lets you tell Git to apply several of those replayed changes as a single combined commit.

Force push

If the remote has different history from your local branch (e.g. because you rebased), you can use:

git push origin main --force

This overwrites the remote branch with your local one. It’s dangerous but useful — it bypasses the usual safeguards and says “make the remote match this branch exactly.” (Prefer --force-with-lease when working with others, as it fails safely if someone else pushed in the meantime.)

  • When you squash commits, you lose the individual commit history (though it’s still recoverable via reflog for a while).

Squashing PRs

Common workflow to squash all commits on a feature branch for a pull request:

  1. Create a new branch off main
  2. Do your work, committing as you go
  3. When ready, squash all commits into one
  4. Push your branch to the remote
  5. Open a pull request into main
  6. Merge once approved

Stash

git stash records the current state of your working directory and the index (staging area) — like a clipboard for uncommitted changes. It stores those changes safely and reverts your working directory to match the HEAD commit.

git stash
git stash list      # list your stashes
git stash pop       # apply and remove the most recent stash

git stash stores changes in a stack (LIFO) structure — you always get the most recent stash first.

⚠️ Don’t leave things stashed for a long time; it’s easy to forget about them.

Multiple stashes

You can stash with a message:

git stash push -m "msg"

You usually won’t need this — if you’re coming back to something much later, it’s better to create a new branch and rebase it later on.

  • Apply a stash without removing it: git stash apply
  • Remove a stash without applying: git stash drop
  • Reference a specific stash: git stash apply stash@{2} (the third most recent) or git stash drop stash@{3}

Revert

A revert is effectively an anti-commit — it doesn’t remove the commit (like reset does) but instead creates a new commit that does the exact opposite of the one being reverted. It undoes the changes while keeping a full history of both the change and its undoing.

git log                 # find the commit hash
git revert <commit-hash>

Diff

git diff shows differences — between commits, the working tree, etc.

  • Difference between the previous commit and current state: git diff HEAD~1
  • Difference between the working tree and the last commit: git diff
  • Difference between two commits: git diff commit_hash_1 commit_hash_2

Revert vs. reset

  • git reset --soft: undo commits but keep changes staged
  • git reset --hard: undo commits and discard changes
  • git revert: create a new commit that undoes a previous one

Use reset when you’re working on your own branch and undoing something you’ve already committed locally. Use revert when undoing a change already on a shared branch — it doesn’t rewrite history, so it won’t disrupt collaborators.

Cherry pick

Use this when you want a specific commit from another branch, without merging or rebasing the whole thing:

git cherry-pick <commit-hash>

You need a clean working tree to do this.

Bisect

How do you find a bug?

  • Revert (common in larger teams)
  • Fail-forward: write a new commit that fixes the bug

How do you find out when a bug was introduced? Instead of manually checking every commit, git bisect does a binary search to find the commit that introduced it.

git bisect isn’t just for bugs — it can find the commit that introduced any change, but bugs and performance regressions are the common use case.

How to bisect:

  1. Start with git bisect start
  2. Mark a known-good commit: git bisect good <commitish>
  3. Mark a known-bad commit: git bisect bad <commitish>
  4. Git checks out a commit between the two for you to test
  5. Run git bisect good or git bisect bad based on the result
  6. Repeat from step 4 until git bisect completes
  7. Exit with git bisect reset

Checking manually each time is tedious — if you have a script that can tell whether the current code is good or bad, automate it:

git bisect run my_script arguments

Don’t forget to make the script executable (chmod +x).

git blame: shows who last changed each line of a file — useful for tracking down context on a change.

Worktree

A worktree is just the directory on your filesystem where the code tracked by Git lives. Usually it’s the root of your repo (where .git lives). It contains:

  • Tracked files
  • Untracked files
  • Modified files

git worktree list — lists all worktrees you’ve created.

Linked worktrees

Worktrees let you work on different changes without losing work. Particularly useful when:

  1. You want to switch back and forth between two change sets without a bunch of git commands (rather than branching or stashing)
  2. You want a lightweight checkout that’s still connected to the main repo

The main worktree:

  • Contains the .git directory with the entire state of the repo
  • Heavy — getting a new main worktree requires git clone or git init

A linked worktree:

  • Contains a .git file pointing to the main worktree
  • Light — about as cheap as a branch
  • Can get complicated with .env files and secrets (since they aren’t tracked/shared automatically)

Create a linked worktree:

git worktree add <path> [<branch>]

<branch> is optional — Git uses the last part of the path as the branch name if omitted.

No duplicate branches: linked worktrees behave like a normal Git repo — you can create branches, switch, delete, tag, etc. But you cannot check out a branch that’s already checked out in another worktree (main or linked).

Upstream

To see if a branch is checked out in another worktree, look for a + next to it in git branch --list.

Delete worktrees

Worktrees are best for long-lived changes, but eventually you’ll need to clean them up:

git worktree remove WORKTREE_NAME

Alternatively, delete the directory manually, then prune:

git worktree prune

Tags

A tag is a name linked to a commit that doesn’t move, unlike a branch. Tags can be created and deleted, but not modified.

List all tags: git tag

Create a tag on the current commit:

git tag -a "tag_name" -m "tag message"

Tags are usually used to mark public version releases.

SemVer

“Semantic Versioning” — a naming convention for versioning software:

v3(major: breaking changes).12(minor: safe new features).5(patch: safe bug fixes)

Two purposes:

  1. A standard convention for versioning software
  2. A signal for how risky/impactful upgrading to a given version will be

Push your tags to your remote GitHub repo:

git push origin --tags

Extra commands

git restore file — discard uncommitted changes to a file

entry.title: Why I use Obsidian Notes
entry.content:
Why you should use obsidian note?

“Your mind is for having ideas, not holding them.” – David Allen

Over the years, I’ve tried many note-taking apps: Evernote, OneNote, Notion, Google Keep… But none of them gave me the level of control, flexibility, and ownership that I found with Obsidian.

🧠 Why I Chose Obsidian

When I started managing multiple technical projects, learning paths, and personal goals, I realized that:

  • I needed something offline and local.
  • I wanted to organize my notes like a second brain, not like a linear notebook.
  • I didn’t want to rely on proprietary formats or platforms.

That’s when I discovered Obsidian. Obsidian stores everything in plain Markdown files. That means:

  • Your notes are yours forever.
  • They’re portable, version-controllable (with Git), and future-proof.


Download Obsidian

📓 A Quick Guide to Markdown

Markdown is the core of Obsidian — it’s a lightweight markup language that makes formatting fast and intuitive. Here are some basics:

Feature Markdown Syntax Example Output
Heading # Title / ## Subtitle / ### H3 Large, medium, small titles
Bold **bold text** bold text
Italic *italic text* italic text
Bold+Italic ***bold italic*** bold italic
Code `inline code` inline code
Code Block ```python
print(“Hello”)
``` (see below)		 Code block
Link [text](https://example.com) my github
Image ![alt text](path/to/image.jpg)
Bullet List - Item 1
- Item 2		 - Item 1
- Item 2
Numbered List 1. First item
2. Second item		 1. First item
2. Second item
Checkbox - [ ] Task
- [x] Done		 - [ ] Task
- [x] Done
Blockquote > Quoted text > Quoted text

Example: Code Block

```python
def greet():
    print("Hello, Markdown!")```

Once you learn Markdown, it becomes second nature. And best of all — it works outside Obsidian too!

🔥 Favorite Features

Here are the features that made Obsidian an essential part of my daily workflow:

1. [[Wikilinks]] and Backlinks

You can easily link notes together using [[note name]], and Obsidian automatically builds a graph of connections. It feels like building your own personal Wikipedia.

2. Graph View 🌐

A beautiful visual representation of how your notes are linked together. Great for seeing the big picture of your knowledge base.

3. Daily Notes + Templates 🗓️

I use Daily Notes to journal tasks, ideas, and thoughts. With templates, I can insert predefined structures — like my morning planning checklist or project logs — instantly.

4. Tags and Search 🔍

Tags help with flexible categorization. Advanced search makes it easy to find any snippet, even in thousands of notes.

5. Plugins Ecosystem 🧩

The community plugins are mind-blowing. Some of my must-haves:

  • Calendar
  • Dataview (query your notes like a database!)
  • Kanban boards
  • Advanced Tables
  • Periodic Notes
  • Tasks Plugin
  • iconize

6. Customizable Hotkeys and Themes 🎨

From light to dark modes, minimal to cyberpunk vibes, you can shape the UI to your taste. I personally use a minimal theme that helps me focus.

7. Local-first + Sync Option

Even though Obsidian is local-first, they offer an optional sync service (paid).

✍️ How I Use Obsidian Daily

  • Studying & Research: I take notes on books, courses, and papers — linking related concepts as I go.
  • Project Management: Each project has its own folder, with meeting notes, todos, and plans.
  • Blog & Content Creation: I draft blog posts (like this one!) in Obsidian before publishing.
  • Personal Knowledge Base: Everything I learn — from cryptography to DevSecOps — lives in my vault.

🧠 Further links

For further information, you can refer to a lot of videos out there, my favourite is this one Obsidian: The King of Learning Tools

Mustapha EL BOUAZAOUI.

entry.title: Comprehensive Guide to Linear Regression: From Theory to Robust Estimation

link.title: Comprehensive Guide to Linear Regression: From Theory to Robust Estimation

entry.content:
Linear Regression: Foundations, Optimization, and Robust Estimation

Author: Mustapha EL BOUAZAOUI
Tags: Machine Learning, Linear Regression, Optimization, RANSAC, Outliers, Gradient Descent, Normal Equation

Linear regression serves as a cornerstone of statistical modeling and supervised machine learning. By establishing a functional relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables, it provides a powerful framework for both prediction and inference. While the concept is conceptually straightforward, a rigorous understanding of its mathematical foundations, optimization techniques, and robust extensions is vital for addressing the complexities of real-world data.

In this article, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the following:

  • The mathematical framework underlying linear regression.
  • The Normal Equation: A closed-form solution, its derivation, and its practical limitations.
  • A probabilistic perspective through Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE).
  • Optimization strategies: Comparing Batch and Stochastic Gradient Descent.
  • Addressing data anomalies: Robust fitting using the RANSAC (Random Sample Consensus) algorithm.
  • Detailed Python implementations and comparative visualizations.

1. Mathematical Foundation of Linear Regression

Problem Setup

Given a dataset of $ n $ observations:
\(\{(x^{(1)}, y^{(1)}), (x^{(2)}, y^{(2)}), \dots, (x^{(n)}, y^{(n)})\}\) where $ x^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^d $ represents the feature vector and $ y^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R} $ is the target variable, our objective is to learn a linear mapping:

\[\hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \theta_2 x_2 + \dots + \theta_d x_d = \theta^T x\]

To evaluate the model’s performance, we employ the Mean Squared Error (MSE) cost function:

\[J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} (\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)})^2\]

The goal of the learning process is to identify the parameter vector $ \theta $ that minimizes $ J(\theta) $.

2. Probabilistic Interpretation: Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Assume the underlying data-generating process follows the form:

\[y^{(i)} = \theta^T x^{(i)} + \epsilon^{(i)}, \quad \epsilon^{(i)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

In this model, the target $y^{(i)}$ is composed of a deterministic linear component and an additive Gaussian noise term. This assumption is frequently justified by the Central Limit Theorem, which suggests that the sum of many independent random errors tends toward a normal distribution.

Under this assumption, the conditional probability of $y^{(i)}$ is given by:

\[P(y^{(i)} | x^{(i)}; \theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} \exp\left(-\frac{(y^{(i)} - \theta^T x^{(i)})^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

For an independently and identically distributed (IID) dataset, the likelihood function is the product of the individual densities:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} P(y^{(i)} | x^{(i)}; \theta)\]

The log-likelihood simplifies this expression for optimization:

\[\log \mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{m}{2} \log(2\pi) - m \log \sigma - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{m} (y^{(i)} - \theta^T x^{(i)})^2\]

Maximizing the log-likelihood with respect to $\theta$ is mathematically equivalent to minimizing the sum of squared residuals:

\[\sum_{i=1}^{m} (y^{(i)} - \theta^T x^{(i)})^2\]

This derivation provides a rigorous statistical justification for the use of Mean Squared Error in linear regression models.

3. Optimization: Gradient Descent

To minimize the cost function $ J(\theta) $, we typically employ gradient descent, an iterative optimization algorithm:

\[\theta := \theta - \alpha \nabla_\theta J(\theta)\]

The method by which we compute the gradient defines the specific variant of the algorithm.

Batch Gradient Descent (BGD)

Batch Gradient Descent utilizes the entire dataset to compute the gradient at each iteration.

\[\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} (\theta^T x^{(i)} - y^{(i)}) x^{(i)}\]

Advantages:

  • Guarantees convergence to the global minimum for convex surfaces.
  • Provides a stable and direct path toward the optimal solution.

Disadvantages:

  • Computationally expensive for very large datasets as the entire matrix must be processed per step.
  • Higher memory requirements.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)

In contrast, Stochastic Gradient Descent updates the model parameters using one sample at a time.

For each observation $ (x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}) $: \(\theta := \theta - \alpha (\theta^T x^{(i)} - y^{(i)}) x^{(i)}\)

Advantages:

  • Significant reduction in computational cost per iteration.
  • The inherent noise in updates can help the model escape shallow local minima in more complex cost surfaces.
  • Enables online learning where the model is updated as new data arrives.

Disadvantages:

  • The parameter trajectory is stochastic (noisy) and may fluctuate around the minimum rather than converging exactly.

Visualization: BGD vs SGD Convergence

The following implementation demonstrates the convergence behavior of both methods on a synthetic dataset.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# Set random seed for reproducibility
np.random.seed(42)

X = 2 * np.random.rand(100, 1)
y = 4 + 3 * X.squeeze() + np.random.randn(100)
X_b = np.c_[np.ones((100, 1)), X]

def batch_gradient_descent(X, y, lr=0.1, n_iters=20):
    theta = np.random.randn(2, 1)
    theta_path = []
    m = len(y)
    for i in range(n_iters):
        gradients = (1/m) * X.T.dot(X.dot(theta) - y.reshape(-1,1))
        theta = theta - lr * gradients
        theta_path.append(theta.copy())
    return np.array(theta_path)

def stochastic_gradient_descent(X, y, lr=0.1, n_epochs=2):
    theta = np.random.randn(2, 1)
    theta_path = []
    m = len(y)
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        for i in range(m):
            xi = X[i:i+1]
            yi = y[i:i+1].reshape(-1,1)
            gradients = xi.T.dot(xi.dot(theta) - yi)
            theta = theta - lr * gradients
            theta_path.append(theta.copy())
    return np.array(theta_path)

theta_bgd_path = batch_gradient_descent(X_b, y)
theta_sgd_path = stochastic_gradient_descent(X_b, y)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
bgd_thetas = theta_bgd_path.squeeze()
plt.plot(bgd_thetas[:, 0], bgd_thetas[:, 1], 'b-s', label='BGD', markersize=4)
plt.title("Batch Gradient Descent Path")
plt.xlabel("Intercept (θ₀)")
plt.ylabel("Slope (θ₁)")
plt.legend()

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
sgd_thetas = theta_sgd_path.squeeze()
plt.plot(sgd_thetas[:, 0], sgd_thetas[:, 1], 'r-o', label='SGD', markersize=2, alpha=0.6)
plt.title("Stochastic Gradient Descent Path")
plt.xlabel("Intercept (θ₀)")
plt.ylabel("Slope (θ₁)")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Analysis: BGD follows a smooth, deterministic path toward the minimum, whereas SGD exhibits more erratic behavior. However, SGD’s ability to process single samples makes it far more scalable for massive datasets.

4. The Normal Equation: Closed-Form Solution

While iterative methods are robust, linear regression admits an analytical solution known as the Normal Equation.

Given a design matrix $ X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} $ and a target vector $ y \in \mathbb{R}^m $, the optimal parameter vector $ \theta $ can be calculated as:

\[\theta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y\]

This equation provides the global minimum of the least-squares objective function in a single step.

Derivation Summary

We aim to minimize the residual sum of squares: $ J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2m}(X\theta - y)^T(X\theta - y) $. Setting the matrix derivative with respect to $\theta$ to zero:

\[\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \frac{1}{m} X^T(X\theta - y) = 0 \Rightarrow X^T X \theta = X^T y \Rightarrow \theta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y\]

Probabilistic Context

As established in Section 2, the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) under the assumption of independent Gaussian noise is precisely the solution provided by the Normal Equation:

\[\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y\]

This reinforces that the least-squares approach is not merely a heuristic but is statistically optimal when errors are normally distributed.

Limitations of the Normal Equation

Despite its efficiency for small datasets, the Normal Equation has significant computational drawbacks:

Challenge Impact
Computational Complexity Inverting $X^T X$ is $O(n^3)$. This becomes prohibitive as the number of features $n$ grows.
Memory Capacity Storing the $n \times n$ matrix $X^T X$ can exceed available RAM for high-dimensional data.
Numerical Instability If $X^T X$ is singular (non-invertible due to multicollinearity), the equation fails.

Feature Scaling and Runtime Performance

We can visualize the performance disparity between the Normal Equation and Gradient Descent as dimensionality increases.


import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import time

def normal_equation_time(X, y):
    start = time.time()
    theta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
    return time.time() - start

def stochastic_gradient_descent_time(X, y, lr=0.01, n_epochs=10):
    start = time.time()
    m, n = X.shape
    theta = np.random.randn(n)
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        indices = np.random.permutation(m)
        for i in indices:
            xi = X[i:i+1]
            yi = y[i]
            gradients = xi.T @ (xi @ theta - yi)
            theta -= lr * gradients
    return time.time() - start

n_samples = 1000
feature_dims = list(range(100, 2100, 200)) + [2500, 3000, 3500, 4000]
ne_times, sgd_times = [], []

np.random.seed(42)

for n_features in feature_dims:
    X = np.random.randn(n_samples, n_features)
    X = np.c_[np.ones((n_samples, 1)), X]
    y = np.random.randn(n_samples)
    X[:, 1:] = (X[:, 1:] - X[:, 1:].mean(axis=0)) / (X[:, 1:].std(axis=0) + 1e-8)

    ne_times.append(normal_equation_time(X, y))
    sgd_times.append(stochastic_gradient_descent_time(X, y))

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plt.plot(feature_dims, ne_times, 'o-', label='Normal Equation')
plt.plot(feature_dims, sgd_times, 's-', label='SGD (10 epochs)')
plt.xlabel('Number of Features')
plt.ylabel('Time (seconds)')
plt.title('Computation Complexity: Normal Equation vs SGD')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

Observation: The cubic growth of the Normal Equation’s runtime makes it unsuitable for high-dimensional feature spaces where SGD maintains linear scalability.

Numerical Instability with Correlated Features

When features are highly correlated, $ X^T X $ becomes ill-conditioned, leading to unstable solutions.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Generate correlated features
np.random.seed(42)
n_samples = 50

x1 = np.random.randn(n_samples)
x2 = x1 + 0.01 * np.random.randn(n_samples)  # Highly correlated with x1

X_corr = np.c_[np.ones(n_samples), x1, x2]
y = 3 * x1 + 2 + np.random.randn(n_samples) * 0.5

# Compute theta using np.linalg.lstsq (more stable)
theta_exact, residuals, rank, s = np.linalg.lstsq(X_corr, y, rcond=None)

# Perturb X and recompute theta
X_perturbed = X_corr + 0.001 * np.random.randn(*X_corr.shape)
theta_perturbed, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(X_perturbed, y, rcond=None)

# Print results
print("Exact solution:", np.round(theta_exact, 3))
print("Perturbed solution:", np.round(theta_perturbed, 3))
print("Difference norm:", np.linalg.norm(theta_exact - theta_perturbed))

# Plot
labels = ['θ₀ (bias)', 'θ₁ (x₁)', 'θ₂ (x₂)']
x = np.arange(len(labels))
width = 0.35

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
bars1 = plt.bar(x - width/2, theta_exact, width, label='Original Data', color='skyblue')
bars2 = plt.bar(x + width/2, theta_perturbed, width, label='Perturbed Data', color='salmon')

plt.axhline(0, color='gray', linewidth=0.8, linestyle='--')

plt.xlabel('Parameter')
plt.ylabel('Coefficient Value')
plt.title('Normal Equation Sensitivity: Correlated Features & Small Noise')
plt.xticks(x, labels)
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, axis='y', alpha=0.3)

# Annotate bars with their heights
def annotate_bars(bars):
    for bar in bars:
        height = bar.get_height()
        plt.annotate(f'{height:.2f}',
                     xy=(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, height),
                     xytext=(0, 5),  # 5 points vertical offset
                     textcoords="offset points",
                     ha='center', va='bottom',
                     fontsize=9)

annotate_bars(bars1)
annotate_bars(bars2)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observation: Tiny changes in data cause large swings in parameters — a sign of numerical instability due to multicollinearity.

When to Use the Normal Equation?

Use Normal Equation When: Use Gradient Descent Instead When:
$ n < 1000 $ features $ n > 10,000 $ features
You need an exact solution You want online/iterative learning
Dataset fits in memory Dataset is too large for $ X^T X $
No multicollinearity Features are correlated or redundant

Note: scikit-learn’s LinearRegression() uses SVD-based solvers (like np.linalg.lstsq) instead of direct inversion to avoid instability.

5. The Challenge of Outliers

One of the primary weaknesses of Ordinary Least Squares is its lack of robustness to outliers. Because the loss function squares the residuals, observations far from the general trend exert a disproportionate influence on the fitted model.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X_outlier = np.vstack([X, [0.1], [1.9]])
y_outlier = np.hstack([y, 15, -5])
X_outlier_b = np.c_[np.ones((102, 1)), X_outlier]

theta_clean = np.linalg.inv(X_b.T.dot(X_b)).dot(X_b.T).dot(y)
theta_noisy = np.linalg.inv(X_outlier_b.T.dot(X_outlier_b)).dot(X_outlier_b.T).dot(y_outlier)

X_line = np.linspace(0, 2, 100)
y_clean_line = theta_clean[0] + theta_clean[1] * X_line
y_noisy_line = theta_noisy[0] + theta_noisy[1] * X_line

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.scatter(X, y, color='blue', label='Inliers', alpha=0.7)
plt.scatter([0.1, 1.9], [15, -5], color='red', s=80, label='Outliers')
plt.plot(X_line, y_clean_line, 'g--', label='Fit on Clean Data')
plt.plot(X_line, y_noisy_line, 'r-', label='Fit on Noisy Data')
plt.title('Impact of Outliers on OLS Estimation')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

Even a small number of severe outliers can significantly tilt the regression line, leading to poor generalization.

6. RANSAC: Robust Regression via Consensus

To mitigate the influence of outliers, we can use RANSAC (Random Sample Consensus). RANSAC is a non-deterministic algorithm that estimates parameters by consensus among a subset of the data.

Theoretical Foundation

RANSAC operates on the assumption that the data contains “inliers” (data consistent with a model) and “outliers” (noise or erroneous data).

The Algorithm:

  1. Selection: Randomly select a minimal set of data points (e.g., two for a line).
  2. Estimation: Fit a model to this minimal subset.
  3. Consensus: Calculate how many points in the entire dataset fall within a distance threshold $\delta$ of this model. These are the inliers.
  4. Iteration: Repeat the process for $k$ trials.
  5. Final Model: Retain the model with the largest consensus (most inliers).

The number of iterations $k$ required to guarantee a successful fit with probability $p$ is: \(k = \frac{\log(1 - p)}{\log(1 - w^n)}\) where $w$ is the expected fraction of inliers and $n$ is the number of points in the minimal subset.

Implementation with Scikit-Learn

While RANSAC can be implemented from scratch, scikit-learn provides a robust and optimized implementation.

import numpy as np

def ransac_linear_regression(X, y, n_samples=2, k_iterations=100, threshold=1.0):
    best_model = None
    best_inliers = None
    max_inliers = 0
    n_points = len(y)
    
    for _ in range(k_iterations):
        # Step 1: Randomly sample minimal set
        idx = np.random.choice(n_points, size=n_samples, replace=False)
        X_sample = X[idx].reshape(-1, 1)
        y_sample = y[idx]
        
        # Step 2: Fit model using Normal Equation
        X_sample_b = np.c_[np.ones(X_sample.shape[0]), X_sample]
        try:
            model = np.linalg.solve(X_sample_b.T @ X_sample_b, X_sample_b.T @ y_sample)
        except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
            continue  # Skip if singular
        
        # Step 3: Predict and find inliers
        y_pred = model[0] + model[1] * X
        inliers = np.abs(y - y_pred) < threshold
        
        num_inliers = np.sum(inliers)
        if num_inliers > max_inliers:
            max_inliers = num_inliers
            best_model = model
            best_inliers = inliers
    
    return best_model, best_inliers

# Example usage
# model, inliers = ransac_linear_regression(X_data, y_data, threshold=2.0)

RANSAC (Random Sample Consensus) is an iterative algorithm that estimates parameters by fitting models to random subsets of data and selecting the one with the most inliers.

using scikit-learn (good for production)

from sklearn.linear_model import RANSACRegressor, LinearRegression

# Define RANSAC with custom settings
ransac = RANSACRegressor(
    estimator=LinearRegression(),
    min_samples=2,                # Minimal points to fit (2 for line)
    residual_threshold=2.0,       # Max residual to be inlier
    max_trials=100,               # Max iterations
    stop_n_inliers=len(X)//2,     # Stop if half are inliers
    random_state=42
)

# Fit model
ransac.fit(X.reshape(-1, 1), y)

# Get inlier mask
inlier_mask = ransac.inlier_mask_
outlier_mask = ~inlier_mask

# Predict
y_ransac = ransac.predict(X.reshape(-1, 1))

Advantages of RANSAC:

  • Highly robust to noise and extreme outliers.
  • Effective even when outliers constitute a significant portion (up to 50%) of the dataset.

RANSAC Visualization

Insight: RANSAC successfully ignores outliers and recovers a line close to the true underlying model.

7. Comparative Summary

Method Best Use Case Key Limitation
Normal Equation Small datasets with few features Scales poorly with dimensionality ($O(n^3)$)
Batch GD Small to medium datasets Can be slow on very large data
Stochastic GD Large scale or streaming data Trajectory is noisy; approximate convergence
RANSAC Datasets with high outlier contamination Increased computational overhead per trial

8. Conclusion

Linear regression remains a foundational tool in the data scientist’s arsenal. By moving beyond simple line-fitting and understanding the probabilistic underpinnings, optimization trade-offs, and robustness techniques, one can build models that are both accurate across clean data and resilient in the presence of noise.

Key Takeaways:

  • Optimization: Choose between exact solutions (Normal Equation) and scalable approximations (SGD) based on data volume.
  • Robustness: Always assess data for outliers and consider consensus-based methods like RANSAC when necessary.
  • Statistical Fidelity: Recall that minimizing MSE is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation under Gaussian assumptions.
